source_text: Περὶ τούτων μὲν μηδὲν προσέχειν συμβουλεύων, μηδὲ εἰ πάνσοφός τις ὑπὸ πάντων ἀνθρώπων μαρτυρηθείη· μόνῳ δὲ προσέχειν Θεῷ, καὶ τοῖς τούτου προφήταις, αὐτὸς ὑποφητεύων καὶ σαφηνίζων, ὅτι ποτὲ σκοτεινὸν καὶ αἰνιγματῶδες ᾖ, οἷα πολλὰ ἐν ταῖς ἱεραῖς ἐστι φωναῖς. ἤτοι οὕτω φίλον ὂν τῷ Θεῷ προσομιλεῖν ἀνθρώποις, ὡς μὴ καὶ ἀναξίαν ψυχήν, οἷαι αἱ πολλαί, γυμνὸς καὶ ἀσκεπὴς ὁ θεῖος εἰσίῃ λόγος· ἢ καὶ τῇ φύσει μὲν σαφέστατον καὶ ἁπλούστατον πάντων τὸ θεῖον λόγιον ὄν· ἡμῖν δὲ ἀποστᾶσι Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀπομεμαθηκόσιν ἀκροᾶσθαι ὑπὸ χρόνου καὶ παλαιότητος, ἀσαφὲς καὶ σκοτεινὸν καταφαινόμενον, οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν. πλὴν σαφηνίζων καὶ εἰς φῶς προσάγων, εἴτε αἰνίγματα ὄντα τυγχάνοι, δεινὸς ὢν ἀκροατὴς Θεοῦ καὶ συνετώτατος· εἴτε καὶ οὐδὲν σκολιὸν ἔχοντα τῇ φύσει, οὐδ᾽ ἀσύνετον αὐτῷ οὕτως ἔχοντι μόνῳ τῶν νῦν ἀνθρώπων, ὧν αὐτός τε ἔγνων, καὶ ἑτέρων ἤκουσα περί τινων λεγόντων, μεμελετηκότι τὰ καθαρὰ τῶν λογίων φωτεινά τε, παραδέχεσθαι αὐτοῦ τῇ ψυχῇ καὶ διδάσκεσθαι ἑτέρους. ὅτι αὐτὸν ὁ πάντων ἀρχηγός, ὁ τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ φίλους προφήτας ὑπηχῶν καὶ ὑποβάλλων πᾶσαν προφητείαν καὶ λόγον μυστικὸν καὶ θεῖον, οὕτως αὐτὸν τιμήσας, ὡς φίλον προσήγορον κατέστησε. ὧν δι᾽ ἑτέρων ᾐνίξατο μόνον, τούτων διὰ τούτου τὴν διδασκαλίαν ποιούμενος. ὅσα τε ἀξιοπιστότατος ὤν, ἢ προσέταξε βασιλικῶς ἢ καὶ ἀπεφήνατο, τούτου τοὺς λόγους διερευνᾶσθαί τε καὶ ἐξευρίσκειν τούτῳ δωρησάμενος· ἵν᾽ εἴ τις σκληρὸς τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ ἄπιστος, ἢ καὶ φιλομαθὴς ὢν τύχοι, παρὰ τούτου μαθών, συνεῖναι καὶ πιστεύειν ἑλέσθαι ἀναγκάζοιτο τρόπον τινά, καὶ ἕπεσθαι Θεῷ. λέγει τε ταῦτα, οὐκ ἄλλως, οἶμαι, ἢ κοινωνίᾳ τοῦ θείου πνεύματος. τῆς γὰρ αὐτῆς δυνάμεως δεῖ προφητεύουσί τε καὶ ἀκροωμένοις προφητῶν. καὶ οὐκ ἂν ἀκούσαι προφήτου, ᾧ μὴ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ προφητεῦσαν, τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν αὐτοῦ λόγων ἐδωρήσατο. τοιοῦτον ἔγκειται λόγιον καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασι, τὸν κλείοντα ἀνοιγνύναι μόνον λέγον, ἄλλον δὲ μηδ᾽ ὁντινοῦν. ἀνοίγει δὲ τὰ κεκλεισμένα, σαφηνίζων τὰ αἰνίγματα ὁ θεῖος λόγος. δῶρον τὸ μέγιστον οὗτος τοῦτο θεόθεν ἔχει λαβών, καὶ μοῖραν παγκάλην οὐρανόθεν, ἑρμηνεὺς εἶναι τῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγων πρὸς ἀνθρώπους, συνιέναι τὰ Θεοῦ, ὡς Θεοῦ λαλοῦντος, καὶ διηγεῖσθαι ἀνθρώποις, ὡς ἀκούσωσιν ἄνθρωποι. τοιγαροῦν οὐδὲν ἡμῖν ἄρρητον· οὐδὲ γὰρ κεκρυμμένον καὶ ἄβατον ἦν. ἐξῆν δὲ καὶ μανθάνειν πάντα λόγον, καὶ βάρβαρον, καὶ Ἕλληνα, καὶ μυστικώτερον, καὶ πολιτικώτερον, καὶ θεῖον καὶ ἀνθρώπινον, σὺν πάσῃ παρρησίᾳ ἐκπεριιοῦσι πάντα καὶ διερευνωμένοις, καὶ πάντων ἐμφορουμένοις, καὶ ἀπολαύουσι τῶν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγαθῶν, εἴτε τι παλαιὸν ἀληθείας μάθημα, εἴτε καὶ ἄλλο τις ὀνομάσαι τοιοῦτον ἔχοι, ἐν αὐτῷ ἦμεν ἔχοντες τὴν θαυμαστήν, καὶ πλήρη τῶν καλλίστων θεαμάτων παρασκευὴν καὶ ἐξουσίαν. καὶ συνελόντα εἰπεῖν, παράδεισος ἡμῖν ὄντως οὗτος ἦν, μιμητὴς τοῦ μεγάλου παραδείσου τοῦ Θεοῦ· ἐν ᾧ γῆν μὲν ἐργάζεσθαι οὐκ ἦν τὴν κάτω, οὐδὲ σωματοτροφεῖν παχυνομένους· τὰ δὲ ψυχῆς μόνον αὔξειν πλεονεκτήματα, ὥσπερ τινὰ φυτὰ ὡραῖα ἑαυτοὺς φυτεύσαντας, ἢ ἐμφυτευθέντας ἡμῖν ὑπὸ τοῦ πάντων αἰτίου εὐφραινομένους καὶ τρυφῶντας.
orientation: Origen teaches them to heed God and His prophets alone, and opens the dark sayings of Scripture.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning these things advising to attend to nothing, not even if someone should be attested all-wise by all men; but to attend to God alone and to His prophets, he himself interpreting as their spokesman and making clear whatever might be dark and riddling, such as many things are in the sacred utterances. Whether it is thus dear to God to converse with men, so that the divine word might not enter naked and uncovered even an unworthy soul, such as most are; or whether, the divine oracle being by nature clearest and simplest of all, to us who have stood away from God and have unlearned to listen through time and antiquity it appears unclear and dark, I am not able to say. Except, making clear and bringing to light, whether they happened to be riddles, being a skilled hearer of God and most understanding; or whether having nothing crooked by nature, not unintelligible to him, being thus disposed alone of men now, of those I myself knew and heard others speaking about, having practiced to receive in his soul the pure and luminous things of the oracles and to teach others. Because the Leader of all, the one who sounds within the friends of God, the prophets, and suggests every prophecy and mystical and divine word, so honoring him made him a friend and one addressed / intimate. What He hinted in riddles through others only, of these making the teaching through this man. And whatever, being most trustworthy, He either commanded royally or declared, granting to this man to search out and discover the reasons of it; so that, if anyone should be hard of soul and unbelieving, or even being eager to learn, learning from this man, he might be compelled in a way to understand and to choose to believe, and to follow God. And he says these things, not otherwise, I think, than by fellowship of the divine Spirit. For of the same power there is need for those prophesying and for those hearing prophets. And one could not hear a prophet, to whom the very Spirit that prophesied did not give the understanding of its words. Such an oracle lies also in the sacred writings, saying that the one who shuts alone opens, and no other whatever. And the divine Word opens the things shut, making clear the riddles. This man has received from God this greatest gift, and a most beautiful portion from heaven: to be an interpreter of the words of God to men, to understand the things of God as God speaking, and to relate them to men so that men may hear. Therefore nothing to us was unspoken/forbidden; for nothing was hidden and inaccessible. It was allowed to learn every doctrine, both barbarian and Greek, both more mystical and more civic, both divine and human, with all freedom going round and searching all, and being filled with all, and enjoying the goods of the soul; whether some ancient learning of truth, or whether anyone could name something else such, in him we were having the wonderful provision and liberty, full of the most beautiful sights. And to say it in sum, this man was truly a paradise to us, an imitator of the great paradise of God; in which it was not to work the earth below, nor to nourish the body growing fat; but only to increase the advantages/riches of the soul, like some fair plants, having planted them ourselves, or having been planted in us by the Cause of all, rejoicing and delighting.

choices.change: Fixed broken English 'as much in the sacred words is' -> 'and much in the sacred words is of that kind' (οἷα πολλὰ … ἐστι).
ἀποστᾶσι Θεοῦ: 'stood apart from God' -> 'fallen away from God'.
οὐδ᾽ ἀσύνετον αὐτῷ: 'not hard to understand for him' -> 'not beyond his understanding'.
τὰ καθαρὰ τῶν λογίων φωτεινά τε: removed the added 'meaning'; now 'what is pure and full of light in the oracles'.
τούτου τοὺς λόγους after plural ὅσα: 'its reasons' -> 'their reasons'.
Speaker: λέγει τε ταῦτα is Origen, but a bare 'He' after sentences about God read as God; now 'And this man says these things'.
Moved 'full of the fairest sights' beside 'store' (it qualifies παρασκευήν).

Translator note corrected: Koetschau also reads μηδέν, not μηδενί. Added Koetschau's compare references (Job 12:14, Genesis 3:23, Matthew 15:13) as uncited possibilities, and listed the print readings followed against Koetschau.
Kept Revelation 3:7 with Isaiah 22:22 (clear allusion) and Genesis 2:8 for 'the great paradise of God' (Eden, confirmed by the 'second Adam out of paradise' that opens section 16).
Kept the sense rendering of ἑαυτοὺς φυτεύσαντας ἢ ἐμφυτευθέντας ἡμῖν (loose grammar, same in Koetschau; disclosed in the note).
Spelling 'counselled' -> 'counseled' (US, to match the book's existing English file).

pass_b_english: In these matters he counseled us to pay no heed at all, not even if someone were attested by all mankind as supremely wise, but to give heed to God alone and to His prophets. He himself acted as their interpreter and made clear whatever was dark and riddling, and much in the sacred words is of that kind. Whether it is God's pleasure to speak with human beings in this way, so that the divine word should not enter naked and uncovered into an unworthy soul, as most souls are; or whether the divine oracle, though by nature the clearest and simplest of all things, appears unclear and dark to us, who have fallen away from God and through the passing of long ages have unlearned how to listen, I cannot say. But he made these things clear and brought them into the light. If they happened to be riddles, he could do so because he was a skilled and most understanding hearer of God; and if they had nothing crooked in their nature, they were not beyond his understanding, since he alone of the people now living, of those I have known myself or heard others speak of, was so disposed, having trained himself to receive into his soul what is pure and full of light in the oracles and to teach it to others. For the Leader of all, who prompts the prophets, the friends of God, and inspires every prophecy and every mystical and divine word, so honored him as to make him His friend and one with whom He speaks. What He had only hinted at in riddles through others, He taught through this man. And whatever He, who is most worthy of trust, either commanded with royal authority or declared, He gave this man the gift to search out and discover their reasons, so that anyone who was hard of soul and unbelieving, or even eager to learn, might learn from him and be compelled, in a way, to understand and to choose to believe, and to follow God. And this man says these things, I think, in no other way than by fellowship with the divine Spirit. For those who prophesy and those who listen to the prophets need the same power; and no one can hear a prophet unless the very Spirit who prophesied gives him understanding of His words. Such an oracle stands written in the sacred Scriptures as well, saying that He who shuts alone opens, and no one else at all (Revelation 3:7; Isaiah 22:22). And the divine Word opens what is shut by making the riddles clear. This man has received from God this greatest of gifts, a most beautiful portion from heaven: to be an interpreter of God's words to human beings, to understand the things of God as though God Himself were speaking, and to explain them to human beings so that they can hear. So nothing was kept from us as unspeakable, for nothing was hidden or barred to us. We were free to learn every kind of teaching, barbarian and Greek, the more mystical and the more concerned with public life, divine and human, going round all of it and searching it out with complete freedom, taking our fill of everything and enjoying the goods of the soul. Whether it was some ancient lesson of truth, or anything else one could call by such a name, in him we had a wonderful store of it, full of the fairest sights, and free access to it. To put it briefly, he was truly a paradise to us, an image of the great paradise of God (Genesis 2:8). There we did not have to till the earth below or feed our bodies and grow fat; we had only to make the soul's riches grow, like fair plants, whether we planted them ourselves or they were planted in us by the Cause of all, while we rejoiced and took our delight.
notes: Copy-text: Vossius / Paris Greek column, printed pp. 72-74, as given in the source row. The print reads Περὶ τούτων μὲν μηδὲν προσέχειν ('to attend to nothing'), as Koetschau 1894 also does; translated as printed ('to pay no heed at all, not even if someone were attested … supremely wise'). 'In these matters' picks up the close of section 14 (human ideas of piety). ὑποφητεύων, the word for one who speaks for an oracle, is rendered 'acted as their interpreter'. The first θεῖος λόγος ('the divine word … naked and uncovered') is taken as God's message and left lower case; the second ('the divine Word opens what is shut') stands beside the Revelation 3:7 key-holder text and is capitalized as Christ the Word. ὁ πάντων ἀρχηγός ('the Leader of all') is capitalized as God; Gregory does not say whether he means the Word or the Spirit. φίλον προσήγορον rendered 'His friend and one with whom He speaks', the same pair as φίλον καὶ προσήγορον Θεῷ in section 12 (where the print's προσήγορον is doubtful). Doubtful print readings: διδάσκεσθαι ἑτέρους, where the sense calls for διδάσκειν, rendered 'to teach it to others'; ἐκπεριιοῦσι read across a line break; μηδ᾽ ὁντινοῦν from a cramped ligature. The print's ἐμφυτευθέντας ἡμῖν (masculine) is loose in grammar; rendered by the sense 'or they were planted in us by the Cause of all'. Scripture: 'He who shuts alone opens' cites Revelation 3:7 (compare Isaiah 22:22; Koetschau also compares Job 12:14); 'the great paradise of God' is Eden (Genesis 2:8). Allusions left uncited as uncertain: 'the prophets, the friends of God' may echo Wisdom 7:27; 'fellowship with the divine Spirit' may echo 2 Corinthians 13:14; tilling the earth and 'fair plants' may echo Genesis 2:9, 2:15 and 3:23 (Koetschau compares Genesis 3:23); plants 'planted … by the Cause of all' may echo Matthew 15:13 (Koetschau compares it). Print readings that differ from Koetschau and were followed: σὺν πάσῃ παρρησίᾳ (Koetschau περιουσίᾳ), ὡς ἀκούσωσιν (Koetschau ἀκούουσιν), προσάγων (Koetschau προάγων), ἁπλούστατον πάντων (Koetschau πᾶν), ὅτι αὐτὸν (Koetschau ὅτε αὐτῶν).
